intro: The beloved is a melody before she is a character: Berlioz’s idée fixe will inhabit a ballroom, disturb a pastoral scene, interrupt an execution march and return grotesquely at the witches’ sabbath. Here, a long, unsettled introduction delays its first full appearance. Listen for the difference between recognising a tune and finding a place where it can rest.
question: How does one melody become an obsession rather than a refrain?

sections.label: Largo introduction
sections.mNote: Hesitant phrases precede the main allegro

sections.label: Idée fixe and allegro
sections.mNote: The beloved’s long melody becomes the principal material

sections.label: Developmental journeys
sections.mNote: The melodic idea travels through changing surroundings

sections.label: Orchestral culmination

cues.title: Before the obsession
cues.text: The symphony begins with an extended slow introduction, not with its famous recurring melody. Listen for phrases that emerge, stop and leave space around themselves. The hesitant beginning matters when the allegro finally gives the beloved a longer musical image.
cues.evidence: Score, movement I, Largo introduction; the recording report shows very low levels and sparse detected attacks through its opening minute. This is a broad opening description, not a bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Silence inside the phrase
cues.text: Follow the spaces between gestures as carefully as the notes. The opening does not sustain one continuous swell: small withdrawals separate its attempts to sing. Try holding the last note in memory while the next phrase is still absent.
cues.evidence: Report: the 0:45 window falls to −50.2 dB, between substantially stronger windows at 0:35 and 0:55.

cues.title: An earlier love song
cues.text: Berlioz says the introduction’s first violin melody came from a romance he wrote as a boy, setting words from Florian’s Estelle. That remembered song is not yet the idée fixe: the score places two different kinds of musical memory beside one another.
cues.evidence: Memoirs, chapter 4, quoted and discussed on the Hector Berlioz Website’s programme and score pages.

cues.title: The introduction stirs
cues.text: The opening’s restraint gives way to more movement and a stronger surge. Do not assume that the main allegro has arrived merely because the music becomes animated: Berlioz makes the introduction itself pass through contrasting states.
cues.evidence: Report: detected attacks increase at 2:00–2:05, and relative level rises from −30.1 dB at 2:00 to −8.6 dB at 2:10. The score still belongs to the introduction.

cues.title: Beethoven in Paris
cues.text: Berlioz heard Beethoven’s symphonies in Paris in 1828. They offered a model of orchestral drama on a large scale. His own five-movement design does not discard that inheritance; it adds a recurring melodic character and an unusually explicit written scenario.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique score commentary, composition history and discussion of Beethoven’s influence.

cues.title: A wandering introduction
cues.text: Listen for the difference between a phrase that settles and one that opens another question. The introduction visits contrasting harmonic regions before the main C-major allegro; its changes of colour are part of the delay, not a sequence of separate movements.
cues.evidence: The score’s extended Largo and changing key signatures establish the introduction’s harmonic travel. No individual modulation is timed here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A second withdrawal
cues.text: Another quieter stretch interrupts the introduction’s earlier force. Keep listening through the reduced sound: this is preparation, not an ending. The eventual allegro will be more striking because the music has made room for it.
cues.evidence: Report: level falls from −23.8 dB at 4:00 to −37.1 dB at 4:10 and remains restrained through the following passage.

cues.title: Harriet before the programme
cues.text: Harriet Smithson’s Shakespeare performances in Paris in 1827 made a powerful impression on Berlioz. The symphony’s artist and beloved are nevertheless figures in a composed scenario: its events are not a diary that can be read literally from the notes.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, composition history: Smithson’s 1827 appearances and the programme’s fictional artist.

cues.title: The idée fixe
cues.text: Around the opening of the allegro, listen for a long melody that reaches forward rather than closing neatly after four bars. The score gives its first full statement to flute and first violins. Remember its outline: later movements change its pace, setting and character.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 71–111, first full idée fixe. The report’s major change at 5:04 and quieter C-major passage from 5:20 locate this region approximately; instrument assignment comes from the score, not the audio measurements.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More than a refrain
cues.text: The idée fixe is not simply a tune that returns between episodes. Berlioz uses it as the first movement’s principal symphonic material: its phrases can be extended, interrupted and developed. Follow what happens to the line, not just whether you recognise its beginning.
cues.evidence: Score commentary: the idée fixe functions as the allegro’s principal subject within a sonata-form design.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Under the singing line
cues.text: Try separating the melody from the activity beneath it. A long upper phrase can sound calm while shorter accompanying figures keep it moving. The important contrast is between musical layers, not simply between loud and soft passages.
cues.evidence: Score, allegro exposition, shows the long idée fixe above shorter accompanying figures. This is a listening strategy for the passage, not an asserted instrumental entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Paris hears the experiment
cues.text: François-Antoine Habeneck conducted the premiere at the Paris Conservatoire on 5 December 1830. Berlioz recalled only two rehearsals. The new work’s unusual sounds therefore reached its first audience under practical conditions far from the finished recording heard here.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Memoirs, chapter 31, on the premiere, conductor and two rehearsals.

cues.title: Energy suddenly withheld
cues.text: A busy stretch gives way to a pronounced withdrawal. Listen to the change in scale: the music can redirect your attention without announcing a wholly new tune. The quieter continuation is another stage of the argument, not a return to the beginning.
cues.evidence: Report: the 7:40–8:00 windows contain 3.6–4.2 detected attacks per second; level then falls from −10.6 dB at 8:00 to roughly −34 dB at 8:05–8:15.

cues.title: A melody in transit
cues.text: The middle of the movement changes the surroundings of familiar material. Ask which fragments still resemble the idée fixe when the accompaniment, register or harmonic setting changes. Recognition here is a matter of contour and rhythm, not identical orchestral colour.
cues.evidence: The score’s development reworks the principal thematic material. No specific fragment or key change is assigned to this second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The sound grows again
cues.text: The quieter middle passage gathers strength rather than remaining a separate oasis. Follow the increasing pressure across several phrases. A crescendo can make a return feel inevitable even before the melody itself becomes unmistakable.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level rises across 8:15–9:15, from −35.0 dB to −10.6 dB, with local reversals rather than a perfectly continuous ramp.

cues.title: Borrowed from Herminie
cues.text: The idée fixe has an earlier life in Berlioz’s 1828 cantata Herminie. Moving it into the symphony changes its job: a vocal idea becomes an orchestral character capable of returning without words across five movements.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique score commentary, identifies Herminie as the source of the idée fixe.

cues.title: Another change of light
cues.text: The music turns away from the preceding sonority before building once more. Listen for continuity beneath the change: the movement’s identity does not depend on keeping the same orchestral weight or remaining in one harmonic region.
cues.evidence: Report: structural-change peaks at 10:32 and 10:40, followed by an increase in level towards 11:35. The measurements locate a change, not its harmonic mechanism.

cues.title: Towards a public voice
cues.text: Compare the vulnerable presentation of the main melody with the movement’s later, weightier rhetoric. The same musical idea can sound private or public according to its scoring and force. Berlioz’s narrative depends on that capacity for transformation.
cues.evidence: Score and programme establish the changing treatment of the principal melody. The comparison concerns large passages rather than a timed statement of the full theme.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The late culmination
cues.text: The late part of the allegro sustains a much stronger sound than its quiet middle. Resist treating every accent as an ending. Listen for the larger span of pressure and for the withdrawal that will eventually release it.
cues.evidence: Report: 11:35–12:00 remains around −6 dB and contains several of the movement’s loudest five-second windows.

cues.title: A last fierce rebound
cues.text: A brief retreat does not yet settle the movement. The sound rebounds strongly before falling away again. This last surge makes the quiet ending a change of manner, rather than merely a gradual loss of volume.
cues.evidence: Report: −34.3 dB at 12:30 rises to −5.7 dB at 12:40; levels then fall markedly after 12:55.

cues.title: A different kind of ending
cues.text: The score’s final Religiosamente asks for a broad, devotional manner. Listen for sustained chords replacing the allegro’s restless activity. The programme calls this religious consolation, but the symphony has four more movements in which to test that apparent repose.
cues.evidence: Score, final Religiosamente; programme, movement I. The report shows sparse attacks and a darker, sustained passage around 13:30–14:00. The cue anticipates that closing region rather than marking its first chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carry the melody onwards
cues.text: Keep the idée fixe in memory as this movement closes. At the ball it will enter a waltz; in the country it will disturb an attempted calm. The later transformations work because this first movement gives the melody enough room to become familiar.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme identifies the beloved’s melody across all five movements; movements II and III describe its intrusion into the ball and pastoral scene.

transitions.title: The long preparation releases
transitions.how: The introduction gathers energy, then makes room for a longer melodic statement. The new allegro establishes a more continuous pulse, but the first full idée fixe is not simply a loud arrival: its relatively restrained opening lets the line itself become the focus.
transitions.evidence: Score, transition into Allegro agitato and bars 71–111. Report: strong change at 5:04, followed by the quieter passage at 5:20. Approximate region, not a bar-synchronised entrance.

transitions.title: Activity gives way to space
transitions.how: A busy stretch withdraws into a quieter continuation. Rather than resetting the movement, the contrast gives familiar material a different scale and harmonic setting. Listen across the drop in volume for a continuing argument.
transitions.evidence: Developmental region of the score; report peak at 8:10 and level fall from −10.6 dB at 8:00 to −35.0 dB at 8:15.

transitions.title: The orchestra gathers force
transitions.how: Changing passages accumulate into a sustained, stronger span. The join is a build-up rather than a clean break: the increased orchestral weight makes the familiar material sound more insistent.
transitions.evidence: Score, late allegro culmination; report rises across 10:40–11:35 and remains near its strongest levels until 12:00. The boundary is an approximate listening division.

transitions.title: Agitation becomes sustained harmony
transitions.how: After a final surge, the active texture subsides. Broad chords and the Religiosamente marking replace the allegro’s forward pressure. The ending changes the way musical time feels; it does not settle the story of the whole symphony.
transitions.evidence: Score, concluding Religiosamente; report shows falling levels after 12:55 and sparse attacks with lower brightness around 13:30–14:00.

facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
